claim: Electroencephalographic recordings from the developing human brain are characterized by spontaneous neuronal bursts, the most common of which is the delta brush.
source: Electroencephalographic recordings from the developing human brain are characterized by spontaneous neuronal bursts, the most common of which is the delta brush.
evidence: This is established knowledge about preterm EEG patterns, supported by the citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Similar events in animal models are known to occur in areas of immature cortex and drive their development.
source: Although similar events in animal models are known to occur in areas of immature cortex and drive their development, their origin in humans has not yet been identified.
evidence: Supported by references to animal model studies cited in the introduction.

claim: The origin of delta brush events in humans has not yet been identified prior to this study.
source: Although similar events in animal models are known to occur in areas of immature cortex and drive their development, their origin in humans has not yet been identified.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Simultaneous EEG-fMRI was used to localise the source of delta brush events in 10 preterm infants aged 32–36 postmenstrual weeks.
source: Here, we use simultaneous EEG-fMRI to localise the source of delta brush events in 10 preterm infants aged 32–36 postmenstrual weeks.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology and sample used in the study.

claim: Left posterior-temporal delta brushes were associated with ipsilateral BOLD activation in the insula only.
source: The most frequent patterns were left and right posterior-temporal delta brushes which were associated in the left hemisphere with ipsilateral BOLD activation in the insula only
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI analysis presented in the study.

claim: Right posterior-temporal delta brushes were associated with BOLD activation in both the insular and temporal cortices.
source: and in the right hemisphere in both the insular and temporal cortices.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI analysis presented in the study.

claim: The insula is one of the most densely connected hubs in the developing cortex.
source: This direct measure of neural and hemodynamic activity shows that the insula, one of the most densely connected hubs in the developing cortex, is a major source of the transient bursting events that are critical for brain maturation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to connectivity studies in the manuscript.

claim: The insula is a major source of the transient bursting events that are critical for brain maturation.
source: This direct measure of neural and hemodynamic activity shows that the insula, one of the most densely connected hubs in the developing cortex, is a major source of the transient bursting events that are critical for brain maturation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing insular activation during delta brushes.

claim: Spontaneous bursts of synchronized neuronal activity (spindle bursts) play an instructive role in key developmental processes in animal models.
source: In animal models, spontaneous bursts of synchronized neuronal activity (known as spindle bursts) play an instructive role in key developmental processes that set early cortical circuits, including neuronal differentiation and synaptogenesis (Hanganu-Opatz, 2010; Khazipov and Luhmann, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references to animal model studies.

claim: Experimental disruption of early spontaneous activity leads to permanent loss of healthy cortical organization in animal models.
source: Experimental disruption of the normal occurrence and propagation of this early spontaneous activity leads to permanent loss of healthy cortical organization, such as segregation into ocular dominance columns (Xu et al., 2011) and whisker barrels (Tolner et al., 2012) in the primary visual and somatosensory cortices respectively.
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental studies in animal models.

claim: Neural activity recorded in human infants during the preterm period with EEG is characterized by intermittent high amplitude bursts known as Spontaneous Activity Transients (SATs).
source: Neural activity recorded in human infants during the preterm period with electroencephalography (EEG) is also characterized by intermittent high amplitude bursts known as Spontaneous Activity Transients (SATs) (Khazipov and Luhmann, 2006; André et al., 2010; Tolonen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: SATs have a crucial role in early human brain development.
source: SATs appear to have a crucial role in early human brain development, as their occurrence is positively correlated to brain growth during the preterm period (Benders et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited study showing correlation with brain growth.

claim: The occurrence of SATs is positively correlated to brain growth during the preterm period.
source: SATs appear to have a crucial role in early human brain development, as their occurrence is positively correlated to brain growth during the preterm period (Benders et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Delta brushes are characterized by a slow delta wave (0.3–1.5 Hz) with superimposed fast frequency alpha-beta spindles (8–25 Hz).
source: The most common of these events is the delta brush, a transient pattern characterised by a slow delta wave (0.3–1.5 Hz) with superimposed fast frequency alpha-beta spindles (8–25 Hz) (André et al., 2010; Whitehead et al., 2017).
evidence: This is the established definition of delta brushes supported by cited references.

claim: Delta brushes appear from 28 to 30 weeks PMA.
source: Delta brushes appear from 28 to 30 weeks PMA (Boylan et al., 2008; Lamblin et al., 1999; Niedermeyer, 2005; Vecchierini et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references describing the developmental timeline.

claim: Delta brushes have a peak incidence at 32–35 weeks PMA.
source: have a peak incidence at 32–35 weeks PMA (André et al., 2010; Boylan et al., 2008; Lamblin et al., 1999; D'Allest and Andre, 2002; Hahn and Tharp, 2005)
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references describing the developmental timeline.

claim: Delta brushes disappear between 38–42 weeks PMA.
source: and disappear between 38–42 weeks PMA (Boylan et al., 2008; Hahn and Tharp, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references describing the developmental timeline.

claim: Delta brushes initially have a diffuse or predominantly peri-central distribution in infants <32 weeks PMA.
source: They initially have a diffuse or predominantly peri-central distribution in infants <32 weeks PMA (Lamblin et al., 1999; Boylan, 2007; Volpe, 1995)
evidence: This is supported by the cited references describing topographical distribution.

claim: Delta brushes progress to have a more temporal and occipital (but rarely frontal) topography in late preterm infants.
source: progressing to have a more temporal and occipital (but rarely frontal) topography in late preterm infants (Tolonen et al., 2007; D'Allest and Andre, 2002; Hahn and Tharp, 2005; Volpe, 1995; Watanabe et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references describing topographical changes.

claim: Delta brushes can be elicited by external stimuli.
source: As with spindle bursts in animal models, delta brushes can also be elicited by external stimuli (Chipaux et al., 2013; Colonnese et al., 2010; Fabrizi et al., 2011; Milh et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental studies.

claim: Delta brush topographies coarsely overlie the primary sensory cortices of the relevant stimulus modality.
source: with their topographies coarsely overlying the primary sensory cortices of the relevant stimulus modality, suggesting that the activation of specific cortical regions appears on the scalp surface as different delta brush distributions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that evoked delta brushes have topographies related to stimulus modality.

claim: Reviewing delta brush incidence and morphology is an important part of the clinical neurophysiological assessment of hospitalised infants.
source: As delta brushes are the hallmark of the preterm EEG, reviewing their incidence and morphology is an important part of the clinical neurophysiological assessment of hospitalised infants (Whitehead et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference on clinical practice.

claim: Preterm infants with a greater incidence of delta brushes are more likely to develop normally.
source: Preterm infants with a greater incidence of delta brushes are more likely to develop normally (Biagioni et al., 1994)
evidence: This is supported by the cited clinical study.

claim: Diminished occurrence or atypical morphology of delta brushes is seen in infants with major brain lesions such as periventricular leukomalacia who later develop cerebral palsy.
source: while diminished occurrence or atypical morphology is seen in infants with major brain lesions such as periventricular leukomalacia who later develop cerebral palsy (André et al., 2010; Watanabe et al., 1999; Conde et al., 2005; Kidokoro et al., 2006; Okumura et al., 1999; Okumura et al., 2002; Tich et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited clinical studies.

claim: Persistent EEG dysmaturity over serial recordings is associated with adverse cognitive outcome.
source: and which is associated with adverse cognitive outcome if persistent over serial recordings (Okumura et al., 2002; Holmes and Lombroso, 1993; Hayakawa et al., 1997; Lombroso, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by the cited clinical studies.

claim: The localization of delta brush sources within the brain cannot be easily inferred just from the electrical potentials recorded at the scalp surface.
source: Whilst delta brushes can be readily identified with EEG, the localization of their source within the brain cannot be easily inferred just from the electrical potentials recorded at the scalp surface (Darvas et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a known limitation of EEG supported by the cited reference.

claim: This study provides the first evidence that spontaneous patterns of delta brush activity are associated with significant hemodynamic activity clearly localized to distinct regions within the developing cortex.
source: Here, we provide the first evidence that spontaneous patterns of delta brush activity in the period preceding normal birth are associated with significant hemodynamic activity clearly localized to distinct regions within the developing cortex.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study based on the experimental data.

claim: The most common event in the late preterm period (posterior-temporal delta brushes) are reflective of activity in the insular cortices and temporal pole.
source: We show that the most common event in the late preterm period (posterior-temporal delta brushes) are reflective of activity in the insular cortices and temporal pole.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI analysis.

claim: Simultaneous EEG-fMRI data were successfully acquired in 10 infants with median PMA at data collection of 35 + 1 weeks (range 32 + 2 to 36 + 2 weeks).
source: Simultaneous EEG-fMRI data were successfully acquired in a group of 10 infants in their late preterm period (median PMA at data collection 35 + 1 weeks, range 32 + 2 to 36 + 2 weeks; five female) during natural sleep over a median of 7.5 min (range: 3.5–10.5 min).
evidence: This describes the study sample and data acquisition parameters.

claim: All infants in the study sample were clinically well at the time of study and were reported as having normal brain appearances on their structural MR images.
source: All the infants in the study sample were clinically well at the time of study and were reported as having normal brain appearances on their structural MR images.
evidence: This describes the clinical characteristics of the study sample.

claim: Delta brushes occurred frequently with a median of 4.4/minute (range: 1.9–6.7).
source: In line with the literature (André et al., 2010; Whitehead et al., 2017), delta brushes occurred frequently (median: 4.4/minute; range: 1.9–6.7)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the EEG analysis.

claim: Delta brushes occurred with 23 different scalp distributions in total.
source: and with varying scalp distributions (23 in total; Figure 1 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Right posterior-temporal delta brushes were consistently present in 10/10 subjects.
source: Nevertheless, right and left posterior-temporal delta brushes were consistently present in 10/10 and in 9/10 subjects respectively
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the EEG analysis.

claim: Left posterior-temporal delta brushes were consistently present in 9/10 subjects.
source: Nevertheless, right and left posterior-temporal delta brushes were consistently present in 10/10 and in 9/10 subjects respectively
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the EEG analysis.

claim: Right and left posterior-temporal delta brushes could be associated with significant clusters of positive BOLD activity (p<0.05 with family wise error correction) in the ipsilateral insular cortex.
source: and could be associated with significant clusters of positive BOLD activity (p<0.05 with family wise error correction) in the ipsilateral insular cortex (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is the primary finding from the fMRI analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The insulae represent major locations of occurrence for developmentally required neuronal events during the late preterm period.
source: This result provides the first evidence that the insulae represent major locations of occurrence for these developmentally required neuronal events during our specific study window in the late preterm period.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The timing and trajectory of maturation differs between brain regions in human preterm development.
source: Although there are rapid changes occurring across the whole brain in human preterm development, the timing and trajectory of maturation has been shown to differ between regions (Makropoulos et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference on brain development.

claim: The insular cortices enter a crucial phase of their development during 32–36 weeks PMA.
source: In agreement with the idea that bursting neural activity is directly linked to brain maturation, the insular cortices in humans enter a crucial phase of their development during our study period (32–36 weeks PMA)
evidence: This is inferred from the cited studies on insular development.

claim: The volumetric growth trajectories of the insular cortices and adjacent temporal lobes accelerate during 32–36 weeks PMA.
source: (i) their volumetric growth trajectories (and those of the adjacent temporal lobes) accelerate (Makropoulos et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference on brain volumetric development.

claim: The insular cortices establish an early pattern of dense functional and structural connectivity during 32–36 weeks PMA, allowing them to assume a prominent role as cortical hubs during infancy.
source: and (ii) they establish an early pattern of dense functional and structural connectivity, which allows them to assume a prominent role as cortical hubs during infancy (Ball et al., 2014; Gao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on connectivity development.

claim: The mature insulae have connections to almost all other regions of the brain.
source: As a result, the mature insulae have connections to almost all other regions of the brain, enabling them to play a versatile role in a wide range of functions including sensory and pain perception, multi-sensory integration, emotion, and cognition (Nieuwenhuys, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference on insular connectivity and function.

claim: The mature insulae play a versatile role in sensory and pain perception, multi-sensory integration, emotion, and cognition.
source: As a result, the mature insulae have connections to almost all other regions of the brain, enabling them to play a versatile role in a wide range of functions including sensory and pain perception, multi-sensory integration, emotion, and cognition (Nieuwenhuys, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference on insular function.

claim: In primates and rodents, the insulae have a dense network of connections and play a key integrative function in sensory and behavioural processes.
source: Similarly, in primates and rodents, the insulae have a dense network of connections and play a key integrative function in sensory and behavioural processes (Butti and Hof, 2010; Mars et al., 2013; Miranda-Dominguez et al., 2014; Zingg et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on insular function in animal models.

claim: The anatomical maturity of the insulae is more advanced in comparison to the surrounding cortex in early life in primates and rodents.
source: Their anatomical maturity is also more advanced in comparison to the surrounding cortex in early life (Huang et al., 2008; Kroenke et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on insular development in animal models.

claim: There are currently no animal developmental studies that directly address the relationship between bursting activity and maturation of the insular cortex.
source: However, there are currently no animal developmental studies that directly address the relationship between bursting activity and maturation of this particular brain region.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the animal model literature.

claim: Right-sided posterior-temporal delta brushes were associated with significant clusters of hemodynamic activity in the right superior temporal lobe and pole.
source: In addition to the insulae, right-sided posterior-temporal delta brushes were associated with significant clusters of hemodynamic activity in the right superior temporal lobe and pole (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The subplate is a transient structure thought to play a fundamental role in the generation of spindle burst activity in animals.
source: This finding is of particular significance as these are regions where the subplate, a transient structure which is thought to play a fundamental role in the generation of spindle burst activity in animals (Tolner et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference on subplate function in animal models.

claim: The subplate can be qualitatively appreciated on high resolution MR images and histology in the superior temporal lobe and pole.
source: can be qualitatively appreciated on high resolution MR images and histology (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) (Kostović et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The subplate reaches maximal thickness in the middle of the third trimester in human development.
source: In human development, the subplate follows a similar trajectory to delta brush activity, reaching maximal thickness in the middle of the third trimester before disappearing in most of the brain by term equivalent age (Kostović et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference on subplate development.

claim: The subplate disappears in most of the brain by term equivalent age in human development.
source: In human development, the subplate follows a similar trajectory to delta brush activity, reaching maximal thickness in the middle of the third trimester before disappearing in most of the brain by term equivalent age (Kostović et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference on subplate development.

claim: The present results support a link between delta brush activity and the subplate in humans.
source: The present results therefore support a link between these functional and structural developmental features in humans.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the temporal and spatial correspondence between delta brushes and subplate.

claim: Source localizing spontaneous delta brushes to the insulae and temporal pole does not necessary imply that this activity starts here.
source: Source localizing spontaneous delta brushes to the insulae and temporal pole does not necessary imply that this activity starts here.
evidence: This is a cautionary interpretation of the findings.

claim: Spindle bursts in animals are recorded from the cortical plate but are thought to be driven by spontaneous activity from the periphery.
source: Spindle bursts in animals are recorded from the cortical plate (Yang et al., 2013), but are thought to be driven by spontaneous activity from the periphery (whisker pad [Yang et al., 2009], spinal cord [Inácio et al., 2016], retina [Hanganu et al., 2006] and cochlea [Johnson et al., 2011])
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on spindle burst generation in animal models.

claim: Spindle bursts in animals are thought to be driven by central pattern generators such as the primary motor cortex, brainstem and thalamus within the somatomotor system.
source: as well as from central pattern generators (CPGs) such as the primary motor cortex, brainstem and thalamus within the somatomotor system (for review see [Luhmann et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is supported by the cited review on spindle burst generation.

claim: It is possible that other neuronal events in peripheral or central centers may precede the occurrence of delta brushes in humans but cannot be detected with EEG and fMRI.
source: It is therefore possible that other neuronal events in these centers may also precede the occurrence of delta brushes in humans, but cannot be detected with EEG and fMRI.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation acknowledging the limitations of the methods.

claim: It is unlikely that the insular activation observed resulted directly from activity in the sensory periphery.
source: Nevertheless, it is unlikely that the insular activation we observed here resulted directly from activity in the sensory periphery as the insulae are not involved in the primary processing of visual (Lee et al., 2012), auditory (Baldoli et al., 2015) or somatosensory stimuli (Allievi et al., 2016; Arichi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the cited studies showing the insulae are not primary sensory areas.

claim: Bilateral and unilateral parietal, occipital and mid-temporal, but rarely frontal, delta brushes were sporadically recorded in individual subjects.
source: Bilateral and unilateral parietal, occipital and mid-temporal, but rarely frontal, delta brushes were also sporadically recorded in individual subjects, suggesting the presence of other less active sources of spontaneous activity at this developmental stage (Figure 3 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The sporadic occurrence of other delta brush topographies suggests the presence of other less active sources of spontaneous activity at this developmental stage.
source: Bilateral and unilateral parietal, occipital and mid-temporal, but rarely frontal, delta brushes were also sporadically recorded in individual subjects, suggesting the presence of other less active sources of spontaneous activity at this developmental stage (Figure 3 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of multiple delta brush topographies.

claim: Areas of BOLD activity were frequently seen in the anatomical homologue in the opposite hemisphere in addition to ipsilateral primary clusters.
source: In addition to the ipsilateral primary clusters, other areas of BOLD activity were also frequently seen in the anatomical homologue in the opposite hemisphere and occasionally in association areas of the cortex (supplementary motor area (SMA), anterior cingulate, precuneus) or deeper structures of the brain (thalamus and basal ganglia) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI analysis.

claim: Areas of BOLD activity were occasionally seen in association areas of the cortex (SMA, anterior cingulate, precuneus) or deeper structures of the brain (thalamus and basal ganglia).
source: In addition to the ipsilateral primary clusters, other areas of BOLD activity were also frequently seen in the anatomical homologue in the opposite hemisphere and occasionally in association areas of the cortex (supplementary motor area (SMA), anterior cingulate, precuneus) or deeper structures of the brain (thalamus and basal ganglia) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI analysis.

claim: Delta brushes with topographies other than posterior-temporal are more frequent earlier on in development compared to the age window studied.
source: Delta brushes with topographies other than posterior-temporal are more frequent earlier on in development compared to the age window studied here (Lamblin et al., 1999; Boylan, 2007; Volpe, 1995)
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on developmental changes in delta brush topography.

claim: Delta brushes with non-posterior-temporal topographies may represent activity from other developing brain regions which follow a different maturational trajectory.
source: and may represent activity from other developing brain regions which follow a different maturational trajectory.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Precise localization of the sources of less common delta brush events will require further work in a larger study population spanning other age ranges.
source: However precise localization of the sources of these events and others that were not recorded in our study group will require further work in a larger study population which spans other age ranges when these regions may be more active.
evidence: This acknowledges the limitations of the current study and suggests future directions.

claim: Longitudinal work may allow exploration of whether key features of spindle burst activity in animals are also present in humans during maturation.
source: Such longitudinal work may also allow an exploration of whether key features of spindle burst activity in animals are also present in humans during maturation, such as increasing propagation of neuronal activity in local and neighbouring networks (Yang et al., 2013) and regional differences in oscillatory patterns (Yang et al., 2009), as well as association of these events to the presence of the transient subplate layer.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research based on animal model findings.

claim: Despite the apparent absence of tight neurovascular coupling in perinatal rodent models, this study demonstrated a clear association between neural (EEG) and positive functional hemodynamic activity (fMRI) in human infants.
source: Despite the apparent absence of a tight neurovascular coupling in perinatal rodent models (Kozberg et al., 2016; Zehendner et al., 2013), we demonstrated for the first time in human infants, a clear association between a direct measure of neural (EEG) and positive functional hemodynamic activity (fMRI).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study contrasting with animal model data.

claim: In rodents, neurovascular coupling matures postnatally together with the development of long-range connectivity patterns.
source: Whilst in rodents, neurovascular coupling matures postnatally together with the development of long-range connectivity patterns (Kozberg et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference on rodent neurovascular development.

claim: In humans, long-range connectivity can be readily identified by the late preterm period, suggesting that neuronal and hemodynamic activity are already closely linked by this time.
source: in humans this connectivity can be readily identified by the late preterm period, thus suggesting that neuronal and hemodynamic activity are already closely linked by this time (Allievi et al., 2016; Doria et al., 2010; White et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the cited studies showing connectivity in preterm infants.

claim: The relationship between neuronal and hemodynamic activity is developmentally regulated across the neonatal period resulting in changing hemodynamic responses.
source: This relationship is developmentally regulated across the neonatal period resulting in changing hemodynamic responses (Arichi et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference on developmental changes in hemodynamic responses.

claim: Neurovascular coupling in neonates is validated by the presence of localised positive BOLD activation in the primary auditory and somatosensory cortices following sound and passive motor stimulation respectively.
source: and is validated by the presence of localised positive BOLD activation in the primary auditory and somatosensory cortices following sound and passive motor stimulation respectively (Allievi et al., 2016; Arichi et al., 2010; Baldoli et al., 2015; Erberich et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by the cited studies showing stimulus-evoked BOLD responses in neonates.

claim: Spontaneous activity is a fundamental feature of developing neural circuits well before the establishment of cortical layers.
source: Spontaneous activity is a fundamental feature of developing neural circuits well before the establishment of cortical layers (Luhmann et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by the cited review on early neural development.

claim: These findings provide the first evidence of a direct link between spontaneous neural and hemodynamic activity in early human life.
source: Our findings provide the first evidence that the most common of these neuronal events in the late preterm period are seen in the posterior temporal regions and are largely generated by the insulae and subplate. As these events are known to have an instructive function in cortical maturation in rodents (Hanganu-Opatz, 2010; Khazipov and Luhmann, 2006; Rakic and Komuro, 1995), our results suggest that these structures may play a key developmental role as a major location of these bursting events in early human life.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the experimental findings.

claim: The insulae and subplate may play a key developmental role as a major location of bursting events in early human life.
source: our results suggest that these structures may play a key developmental role as a major location of these bursting events in early human life.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization findings and the known role of bursting activity in development.

claim: Thirteen preterm infants were recruited for the study from the Neonatal Unit at St Thomas' Hospital, London.
source: Thirteen preterm infants (five females; studied between 32–36 weeks post-menstrual age, PMA) 5–55 days old (23 ± 17, mean ±SD) were recruited for this study from the Neonatal Unit at St Thomas' Hospital, London (patient demographic information is detailed in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the study recruitment.

claim: Infants were excluded if they required any respiratory support during scanning or if they were known to have a history of severe brain pathology.
source: Infants were excluded if they required any respiratory support during scanning or if they were known to have a history of severe brain pathology such as extensive intraventricular hemorrhage (grade 3 with ventricular dilatation; grade 4 with parenchymal extension), birth asphyxia, focal intracerebral lesions affecting the parenchyma or white matter (such as infarction, overt hemorrhage, or multiple punctate white matter lesions), severe hydrocephalus, or congenital brain malformations.
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria for the study.

claim: An optimized pre-processing and analysis pipeline which incorporated an age-specific hemodynamic response function (HRF) and template brain was used for the fMRI data.
source: An optimized pre-processing and analysis pipeline which incorporated an age-specific hemodynamic response function (HRF) and template brain was used for the fMRI data (detailed in the supplementary methods) (Allievi et al., 2016; Arichi et al., 2012; Arichi et al., 2010; Serag et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: Inter-rater reliability for delta brush identification resulted in substantial agreement with median Fleiss' Kappa 0.65 (range 0.25–0.76).
source: Inter-rater reliability was assessed using Fleiss' Kappa analysis (Fleiss, 1971) and resulted in a substantial agreement (median Fleiss' Kappa 0.65 (range 0.25–0.76)).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of the reliability of the EEG analysis.

claim: Two data sets were discarded because of insufficient EEG quality.
source: Two data sets were discarded because of insufficient EEG quality (due to bridging electrodes or unsuccessful artifact removal) which made them unsuitable for reliable delta brush detection.
evidence: This describes data exclusion from the analysis.

claim: One data set was discarded as the remaining data segment did not contain more than 3 delta brushes with the same topography.
source: One data set was discarded as the remaining data segment did not contain more than 3 delta brushes with the same topography (i.e. belonging to the same EV).
evidence: This describes data exclusion from the analysis.

claim: Right posterior-temporal delta brush activity was significantly associated with BOLD clusters in the right temporal pole, right superior temporal lobe, and the right insular cortex.
source: In a group of 10 preterm infants (35 + 0 weeks PMA, range 32 + 2 to 36 + 2 weeks), right posterior-temporal delta brush activity (blue) was significantly associated with BOLD clusters in the right temporal pole (z50, z55), right superior temporal lobe (x28), and the right insular cortex (z60, z62, z64, z66).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 and represents the group-level fMRI findings.

claim: Left posterior-temporal delta brush activity was significantly associated with BOLD clusters in the left posterior insula and left parietal operculum.
source: Left posterior-temporal delta brush activity (red-yellow) was significantly associated with BOLD clusters in the left posterior insula (z64, z66) and left parietal operculum (z66, z68).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 and represents the group-level fMRI findings.

claim: The degree of prematurity at birth adversely affects both insular volume and thalamo-insular connectivity at term equivalent age.
source: The importance of the preterm period for insular development in humans is further emphasized by studies showing that the degree of prematurity at birth, recreational drug use in pregnancy and late onset intra-uterine growth restriction adversely affects both insular volume and thalamo-insular connectivity at term equivalent age (Ball et al., 2012; Batalle et al., 2016; Egaña-Ugrinovic et al., 2014; Grewen et al., 2015; Salzwedel et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on the effects of prematurity on insular development.

claim: Recreational drug use in pregnancy adversely affects both insular volume and thalamo-insular connectivity at term equivalent age.
source: The importance of the preterm period for insular development in humans is further emphasized by studies showing that the degree of prematurity at birth, recreational drug use in pregnancy and late onset intra-uterine growth restriction adversely affects both insular volume and thalamo-insular connectivity at term equivalent age (Ball et al., 2012; Batalle et al., 2016; Egaña-Ugrinovic et al., 2014; Grewen et al., 2015; Salzwedel et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on the effects of drug use on insular development.

claim: Late onset intra-uterine growth restriction adversely affects both insular volume and thalamo-insular connectivity at term equivalent age.
source: The importance of the preterm period for insular development in humans is further emphasized by studies showing that the degree of prematurity at birth, recreational drug use in pregnancy and late onset intra-uterine growth restriction adversely affects both insular volume and thalamo-insular connectivity at term equivalent age (Ball et al., 2012; Batalle et al., 2016; Egaña-Ugrinovic et al., 2014; Grewen et al., 2015; Salzwedel et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on the effects of growth restriction on insular development.

claim: Thalamo-insular connectivity at term equivalent age is significantly correlated with cognitive outcome at 2 years of age.
source: with the latter being significantly correlated with cognitive outcome at 2 years of age (Ball et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference on the relationship between connectivity and outcome.

claim: Insular dysfunction and poor growth have been implicated in a range of psychiatric conditions, including neurodevelopmental difficulties such as autism spectrum and attention deficit hyperactivity disorders.
source: Furthermore, insular dysfunction and poor growth have been implicated in a range of psychiatric conditions, including neurodevelopmental difficulties such as autism spectrum and attention deficit hyperactivity disorders which have greater prevalence in preterm born children (Hatton et al., 2012; Johnson and Marlow, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on insular involvement in psychiatric conditions.

claim: Autism spectrum and attention deficit hyperactivity disorders have greater prevalence in preterm born children.
source: Furthermore, insular dysfunction and poor growth have been implicated in a range of psychiatric conditions, including neurodevelopmental difficulties such as autism spectrum and attention deficit hyperactivity disorders which have greater prevalence in preterm born children (Hatton et al., 2012; Johnson and Marlow, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on outcomes in preterm children.
